title: Prayers for others
hook: blessings for the sick, the community and the country

segments.voice: Yesterday, the haftarah, the reading from the Prophets. Your line was the prophets answer. Did a later voice answer an old story for you? Today, the prayers said around the open scroll, for other people. Day six hundred one.

While the Torah lies open on the table, there's a pause between readings. Someone walks up to the person leading and whispers a name. Then another. Then a list on a scrap of paper. A neighbor's husband after surgery. A cousin's newborn. A friend in rehab. The leader starts a short prayer, and when it reaches the gap, the names pour in, sometimes for a full minute. In some congregations, people simply stand and say them out loud, one after another, until the room goes quiet again.
screen: `A NAME WHISPERED TO THE LEADER.` → `A LIST ON A SCRAP OF PAPER.` → `THE NAMES POUR IN.`

segments.voice: The prayer begins Mi sheberach avoteinu: may the One who blessed our ancestors, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in many communities Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, bless this person. It's a formula, a frame, and almost anything can go in it. There's a Mi Sheberach for each person called up to the Torah. A Mi Sheberach for the sick, asking for complete healing of body and spirit, where you'll hear the names from that scrap of paper. One for the whole congregation, and for everyone who gives to it and serves it. One for a new baby, one for a couple about to marry. Many synagogues also say a prayer for the country and its leaders, and in many communities one for the State of Israel and those who defend it. Praying for the government has deep roots. When the prophet Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon, he tells them, in the old Jewish translation: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Not Jerusalem, the city they lost. Babylon, the city that took them captive. And in Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests, says to pray for the welfare of the government, because without it, people would swallow one another alive. In recent decades the songwriter Debbie Friedman wrote a sung version of the prayer for healing, and some synagogues now sing it in place of the spoken one. The frame stays the same: the blessing that reached our ancestors, asked for someone else.
screen: `MAY THE ONE WHO BLESSED OUR ANCESTORS.` · `FOR THE SICK, THE CALLED UP, THE NEW.` · `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · `PRAY FOR THE GOVERNMENT'S WELFARE.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your town. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place you live: the main street, the school, the hospital, the bus stop, the people you pass without knowing their names. Picture the people who run it, the ones you voted for and the ones you didn't. Hold one wish for the whole place: safety, fairness, enough. If you pray, you can ask for its peace. If not, just let yourself care, for a minute, about people you'll never meet. The bell holds the time.
Mi Sheberach. May the One who blessed. The prayer said around the Torah for the sick, the congregation, and the country.
Your line: pray for the city. Today, do one small thing for your town: pick up litter, thank a bus driver, read one local news story all the way through. Day six hundred one.

howItsDone: During the Torah service, Mi Sheberach blessings are said for those called up, for the sick, whose names are added aloud or whispered to the leader, and for the congregation; many synagogues also say prayers for the country and for the State of Israel.

fork.setup: you're an exile in Babylon. a letter arrives from the prophet Jeremiah. what does it tell you to do about Babylon?
options: curse it and wait to leave.
seek its peace and pray for it.
ignore it and keep to yourselves.
fork.reveal: seek the peace of the city, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

original.note: Hebrew: the One who blessed. the opening words of the prayer for others.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prayer for sick people.
what it means: a frame for blessing others, from the sick to the whole country, asking the ancestors' blessing for someone else.
what a scholar hears: Jeremiah 29:7; Pirkei Avot 3:2, Rabbi Chanina segan hakohanim; prayers for the government in medieval siddurim (Hanoten teshuah); Debbie Friedman's sung version.

sources.ref: Mi Sheberach prayers in the Torah service

notes: Jeremiah 29:7 quoted as JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Pirkei Avot 3:2: Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests; paraphrased.
Debbie Friedman's Mi Shebeirach (written around 1987) is named but not quoted (it is under copyright).
Prayer for the State of Israel and its defenders is said in many but not all communities; described as 'in many communities'.
The tomorrow title 'Our duty to praise' (Aleinu) follows the outline.

Editor review (y2 595–612): the garbled 'Not your city. Their city.' now says plainly that Jeremiah meant Babylon, not Jerusalem; 'has become loved in many synagogues' (unsourced) softened to 'some synagogues now sing it'.
